paragraphs: Sometimes the market price of a product goes up because of rules from the state. This higher price can last as long as these rules last.

The market price of a product can stay above its natural price for a long time. But it can rarely stay below its natural price for long. Why is this? If people get less than the natural price, they lose money. They feel this loss very quickly. So they stop using so much land, work or money for this product. Then less of the product comes to the market. Soon there is only enough for the people who want it and can pay for it. So the market price goes up again to the natural price. This is true at least when there is perfect freedom.

There are old laws about apprentices and about trade groups. An apprentice is a young person who learns a job from a master. When a trade is doing well, these laws help the worker. He can push his pay far above its natural level. But when the trade is doing badly, the same laws can push his pay far below it. In good times, the laws keep many people out of his trade. In bad times, they keep him out of many other trades.

But the effect is not the same in both cases. The laws can keep pay high for many hundreds of years. They cannot keep pay low for so long. Low pay lasts only while some workers are still alive. These are the workers who learned the trade in the good times. When they are gone, new people learn the trade. Their number will then match the real demand. Only very hard rules can keep the pay for work or the profits of money below their natural level in one job for many generations. There were rules like this in Indostan and in ancient Egypt. There, religion told every man to do the same job as his father. Changing to another job was a terrible crime against God.
That is all I need to say for now about the market price. Sometimes it moves away from the natural price for a short time, and sometimes for a long time.

The natural price also changes. It has three parts: wages, profit and rent. Wages are the pay for work. Each part has its own natural level. In every country this level changes with the situation of the country. Is the country rich or poor? Is it growing, staying the same, or getting weaker? In the next four chapters, I will try to explain the causes of these changes. I will do it as fully and clearly as I can.
First, I will try to explain what decides the level of wages. I will also show how these things change in a rich or poor country, and in a country that is growing, staying the same or getting weaker.
Second, I will try to show what decides the level of profit. I will also show how the same changes in a country affect these things.
